I think that's fine. I didn't come up with the rules, but here it is in the FAQ:

Can I submit links to sites I operate?

Submitting only links to sites you operate (or are associated with), without submitting other, unrelated links, is considered spamming. If you submit niche content (for example gaming videos from your own YouTube channel), you should create your own subverse and submit the content only to that subverse. If majority of the links you submit are to sites you are associated with, your domains may be globally banned from Voat. To be on the safe side, if you submit 10 links to various subverses on Voat, at most 5 of the 10 submitted links may be to the sites you are associated with.

So it's a 50/50 thing, and I think it only applies if you post to popular, high-activity subverses. Wards off advertisers and keeps content a little more varied.

Submitting only links to sites you operate (or are associated with), without submitting other, unrelated links, is considered spamming.

I saw that FAQ, but got the impression that it is often not possible to decide whether an user is a spammer or not, because domain ownership/association with specific user cannot be determined.

I take issue with the phrasing as well, but sometimes it is obvious. For instance, /u/website-dot-com exclusively posting links to website.com. Still, that is far from 100% of domain spam cases. I think the clause should be re-written to exclude association or ownership from the matter at all, and simply forbid the exclusive posting of any one domain type. Only thus can domain spam be prevented without having to make impossible judgments about association. And it helps keep content varied and forces users to put a little more effort into submitting (which may be good in terms of quality, but bad in terms of quantity, as it may discourage posting entirely).

The Happenings - See You In September

This was first released by The Tempos in 1959, reaching #23. It has a much more "cha-cha" flavor to it. The Happenings released this in 1966 and reached #3. It was written by Sid Wayne and Sherman Edwards, Sid would recall the song's inception: "I was in the habit of going from my home on Long Island every day to Brill Building, on Tin Pan Alley [to] and meet with different songwriters there. We'd eat at Jack Dempsey's or The Turf Restaurant and then we'd go up to one of the publishers' offices and work in the piano room. We'd sit around saying to each other, 'What do you want to write today? A hit or a standard?'" At 11 a.m. on a Friday in June 1959 Wayne thus met up with Sherman Edwards: "he said, 'What do you want to write?' 'I'd like to write a song called See You in September,"' I said. We talked it back and forth and I think I may have contributed part of the opening music, but with Sherman it didn't matter, because he could throw me back half the lyric — that's how he worked. I think probably by two in the afternoon we got the song finished. It needed to be written; it was like boiling inside of us."

By 4:30 p.m. that day, Wayne and Edwards had reworked their composition, simplifying it so as to appeal to the teen demographic, and proceeded to make the rounds of publishers to pitch the song which, after one rejection, met with an enthusiastic reception from Jack Gold, owner of the local Paris label, who by 8 p.m. had telephoned the Tempos in their hometown of Pittsburgh. The group had been flown into New York City by the next day, Saturday. Sid Wayne: "By Monday the record was cut [with the Billy Mure orchestra], test pressings were Thursday, and by Friday the song was played on WNEW in New York. The thing took off like wildfire… Five hundred dollars to split between the two of us [ie. Wayne & Edwards]… was a damn good week's pay in 1961."

Bob Miranda of the Happenings recalls that he and the other members of the group considered the original version of "See You in September", a great song and kind of a bad record. We always looked for that. If you want to revise something and put your own sound to it, I think you should look for a great song that was not a great record."
